notes:
I've written notes for most verses of Daniel 10, but there are some gaps you should know about first. My page-fetch tool stopped working on the first try, so I never opened a full page. Every note below comes from the long excerpts the search tool returned, so some commentators' notes on some verses are missing. I also ran out of searches before reaching the Catholic and Orthodox sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org), bibleodyssey.org, and the Lutheran, Wesleyan, Pentecostal and Baptist-preacher sites. Those sections are mostly left out, as you asked.

**About the tradition labels:** StudyLight tags Gill as "Baptist · Calvinism" and Wesley's Notes as "Arminian." Every other tradition label in brackets is my own general identification; the pages don't give it.

---

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- **The date and Daniel's age.**
  - The NET Bible notes say chapters 10–12 are one closing unit that the chapter breaks partly hide. They date Cyrus's third year to about 536 BC, when Daniel would have been about 84. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Dan&chapter=10&verse=1
  - Gill, following Prideaux, works it out to about 91 and thinks Daniel probably died soon after. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
- **"Great conflict" (Hebrew *tsava*).**
  - NET says the word is uncertain here. It usually means army or warfare, but many take it as "hard service." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Dan&chapter=10&verse=1
  - Ellicott reads it as the tribulation that all God's people must go through before the Messiah's kingdom. He also notes that Daniel 12:8 shows Daniel did not understand everything. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
  - Clarke reads it as "the warfare long": many wars before the prophecy is fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/daniel-10.html
  - Constable says the KJV's "time appointed was long" has weaker language support, though the prophecy did reach far into the future. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- **"The message was true."**
  - Gill: a real revelation, not a fancy or like pagan fortune-telling. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says Daniel gives this assurance because Daniel 11 is so detailed that people are tempted to treat it as written after the events. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-10.html
  - Precept Austin answers the claimed clash with Daniel 1:21: that verse doesn't say Daniel died then, only that he lived to see the year of return. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary

**vv. 2–3**
- **Why Daniel mourned.**
  - Ellicott links it to the troubles of the exiles who had gone back (Ezra 4), to how few had returned, and to the Levites who chose to stay in Babylon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
  - Constable gives similar reasons: earlier revelations and opposition in the land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- **The fast itself.**
  - NET: the Hebrew says "three weeks of days," perhaps to set these apart from the "weeks of years" in chapter 9. Oil was linked with rejoicing, so people usually didn't use it while mourning. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Dan&chapter=10
  - Gill: Daniel gave up fine bread, delicate meat and good wine for coarse food, to give himself to devotion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
  - Matthew Henry: Daniel ate little and plainly, which "may truly be reckoned fasting." Good people grieve at how slowly God's work moves. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_010.cfm
  - Precept Austin presents Daniel as an intercessor "standing in the gap" for God's people. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary

**v. 4**
- **Passover.** NET says the first month is Nisan, the month of Passover. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Dan&chapter=10
  - Gill thinks the fast ran from the 3rd to the 24th, so it covered Passover, which may not have been kept in exile. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
  - Constable agrees that the feasts weren't kept as before during captivity. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- **The river.** Ellicott: Hiddekel is the Tigris, and "great river" usually means the Euphrates. Daniel was there in body, not only in vision as in 8:2. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
  - Pulpit agrees, pointing to the men who were with him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/daniel/10.htm

**vv. 5–6: Who is the "man dressed in linen"? (the main point where traditions differ)**
- **He is the pre-incarnate Christ:**
  - Gill [Baptist]: "not Gabriel, but the Son of God." The linen points to Christ as priest, and each feature of his body is read as one of Christ's qualities. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-6.html
  - Matthew Henry [Presbyterian]: this is Christ, because he looks the same as in John's vision (Revelation 1:13–15). His dress is a high priest's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_010.cfm
  - Poole [Puritan]: Christ, shown in royal and priestly robes "not proper for any angel." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-5.htm
  - Trapp: the Messiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jtc/daniel-10.html
  - Ellicott [Anglican]: he is not Michael and apparently not Gabriel. He is the "Angel of God" or "God's Presence," in fact the Logos. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
  - Chuck Smith says the descriptions match Revelation 1 so closely that many affirm it is Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-5.html
- **He is an angel:**
  - Calvin [Reformed]: an angel in human form. Calvin calls the linen-equals-Christ's-priesthood reading a refinement "destitute of all reality." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-5.html
  - The Geneva notes: "the angel of God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-5.htm
  - Barnes: an angel. Another entry on the same Bible Hub page says he is an angel of the highest order, because in 8:16 he gives orders to Gabriel. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-5.htm
  - NET: presumably an unnamed angel, with "no adequate reason" to call him Gabriel. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Dan+10%3A5%2C6%2C18
  - Clarke [Methodist] notes the likeness to Revelation 1 at 10:6 (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/daniel-10.html), but at 12:6 he says this figure is Gabriel (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/12-6.html).
- **Undecided or mixed views:**
  - Enduring Word (Guzik) says commentators are divided. Some see Jesus because of Revelation 1. Others see a high-ranking angel, since Jesus would not need Michael's help (v. 13). Guzik lines the two descriptions up side by side and notes that Ezekiel saw angels in linen. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/ ; https://blueletterbible.org/Comm/guzik_david/StudyGuide_Dan/Dan_10.cfm?a=860011
  - Constable sides with Walvoord: the figure in vv. 5–6 is God, but the speaker in vv. 10–21 is an angel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- **Details of the description:**
  - Uphaz's location and even its exact name are uncertain; some scholars change it to *paz*, "pure gold." *Tarshish* may be yellow jasper. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Dan+10%3A5%2C6%2C18
  - Ellicott: the "feet" are the lower limbs. In 12:6 the figure is above the waters, picturing God as supreme over the nations. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
  - The Cambridge Bible says the linen picture probably comes from Ezekiel 9–10. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-5.htm
  - The Layman's Bible Commentary says the description is modelled on Ezekiel's vision of God (Ezekiel 1). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/daniel-10.html

**v. 7**
- Enduring Word compares Paul's companions on the Damascus road: people can be close to God's power and still miss the message. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/
- Ellicott notes that Jerome made the same comparison (Acts 22:9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
- Gill thinks the men were probably Daniel's pagan servants, not his three friends or the prophets that rabbinic tradition suggests. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-7.html
- Henry: many have "a spirit of bondage to fear" without the spirit of adoption. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_010.cfm
- Precept Austin: Daniel saw because God opened his eyes to the supernatural. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: this vision was more glorious than the earlier ones, and Daniel went pale and fainted. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/daniel/10.htm
- Henry: even the best people cannot bear a direct sight of God's glory. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_010.cfm
- Enduring Word: even godly Daniel was undone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/

**v. 9**
- Gill: Daniel fell either in worship or from faintness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
- Precept Austin: this suggests he lost consciousness, and lying face down fits "if this is indeed a Christophany." https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60041/

**v. 10**
- **Whose hand was it?**
  - Ellicott: the same person's, felt but not seen. The verb can mean "shook," so Daniel was crouching and trembling. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-10.html
  - Gill: a different person, probably Gabriel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html
- Henry: strength returns by degrees. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Dan/Dan_010.cfm

**v. 11**
- NET: "highly precious" can be "a treasured person." "Stand up" is literally "stand upon your standing." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php/o/w/passage.php?passage=Dan+10%3A5%2C6%2C11%2C12
- Enduring Word: this is the second time Daniel is called "greatly beloved" (after 9:23), each time with a major revelation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/
- Gill: being "sent" shows the speaker is an angel, not the glorious figure of vv. 5–6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/daniel-10.html

**v. 12**
- Gill: the prayer was heard and the answer ordered on the very first day. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-12.html
- Enduring Word: this shows that prayer is not just therapy; it "moves heaven to action." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/
- Precept Austin, quoting Strauss: a delayed answer is not a denied one. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary

**v. 13: The prince of Persia and Michael**
- **Who is the "prince"?**
  - Most say an evil angel:
    - Gill: not Cyrus and not a good angel, but Satan or one of his chief angels at the Persian court. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-13.html
    - Ellicott: "devils" (1 Corinthians 10:20) who influenced Cyrus against Israel during the Samaritan plots. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html
    - Ironside and Constable take the same view. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/isn/daniel-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
  - Poole notes that some take it as earthly princes, and asks who could imagine good angels fighting each other. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-13.htm
  - Bible Hub's unsigned Q&A article cites Jerome for the angelic reading. https://biblehub.com/q/Who_is_the_prince_in_Daniel_10_13.htm
- **Who is Michael?**
  - Gill: Michael is Christ himself, an "uncreated Angel." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-13.html
  - Ellicott and JFB say no. "First prince" shows that, great as he is, he is nothing compared with God, and JFB notes that his name means "Who is like God?" https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-13.html
- **"I had been left there."**
  - Ellicott reads "I prevailed there." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html
  - Theodotion's Greek reads "I left him [Michael] there," and some English versions follow it. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=Dan+10%3A13-21
  - Gill calls that reading wrong. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-13.html
- **The 21 days and persistent prayer.**
  - Enduring Word: the 21 days match Daniel's fast, so if he had stopped on day 20 the answer might not have come. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/
  - Keil & Delitzsch and Barnes also equate the 21 days with the fast. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-13.html
- **Popular "spiritual warfare" practice.** Constable warns that nothing in the Bible supports praying against demons by name and "claiming victory" over them. Daniel did not even know about the battle, and Michael's success did not come from his prayers. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
  - By contrast, Bible Hub's Q&A calls the prince a "territorial spirit." https://biblehub.com/q/Significance_of_Prince_in_Daniel_10_20.htm

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: "those days" means the time when Daniel 11 is fulfilled. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html
- Precept Austin calls this the key verse of chapters 10–12 and reads it as Israel's future. It rejects the view that the church replaces Israel. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary
- Constable: the earlier revelations (8:23–26; 9:24–27) had puzzled Daniel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html

**v. 15**
- Ellicott: this is reverence and gratitude, not fear, which had already been removed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html

**v. 16**
- NET: one Hebrew manuscript, the Dead Sea Scrolls and the Septuagint read "something that looked like a man's hand." "My lord" is a polite title. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Dan&chapter=10
- Ellicott sees no reason to think this is a different person from vv. 10 and 18. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html
- Enduring Word: this was an angel, not God; God touched Daniel through a go-between. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/daniel-10/

**v. 17**
- Ellicott compares Isaiah's fear in Isaiah 6:5. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html

**v. 18**
- Pulpit: it is not reading too much in to see the repeated man-like figure as a symbol of Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/daniel/10.htm
- Pulpit's sermon notes: God comes to us through Christ's brotherly sympathy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/daniel-10.html
- Gill: God's power came with the angel's comforting words. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-18.html

**v. 19**
- Constable compares Joshua 1:9. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- Precept Austin: the encouraging words themselves gave Daniel inner strength. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary

**v. 20**
- NET: the question is rhetorical, meant to make Daniel reflect. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Dan&chapter=10
- Ellicott calls the verse obscure. He reads "gone forth" in a military sense. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html
- Gill: Satan kept working against the Jews at the Persian court, and later through Alexander's successors and especially Antiochus. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-20.html
- Constable: the prince of Greece may point to Alexander the Great. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- Two unnamed entries on the Bible Hub page:
  - One says "prince of Persia" may mean the human ruler, such as Cambyses.
  - The other sees a new demonic opponent, pointing ahead to Antiochus Epiphanes and the Antichrist.
  - https://biblehub.com/commentaries/daniel/10-20.htm

**v. 21**
- NET: "a book of truth"; "your" is plural, so Michael is the angelic prince of Daniel's whole people. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Dan&chapter=10
- Gill: the "book" is God's decrees, not Scripture, and "Michael your prince" is Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/daniel/10-21.html
- Constable: it is everything God has recorded as truth, including things he has not revealed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/daniel-10.html
- Ellicott: don't despair as one persecuting empire follows another; it is all written down already. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/daniel-10.html

---

## Other views (only what I could find)
- **Modern scholarship:** I found no bibleodyssey.org material.
  - Precept Austin argues against the view that a 2nd-century-BC Maccabean author wrote the book, saying such a writer would have placed Daniel in Judea. https://www.preceptaustin.org/daniel_10_commentary
  - The Layman's Bible Commentary treats the scene as drawing on Ezekiel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lbc/daniel-10.html
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I only found Jerome as reported by others: Ellicott for v. 7, and Bible Hub's Q&A for v. 13. Neither is from a Catholic or Orthodox site.

If you'd like, I can try again later to fill the gaps: the Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran, Wesleyan, Pentecostal and modern-scholarship sites, and full pages for Calvin, Wesley's Notes and Keil & Delitzsch.
